cards.title: Cloud KMS — Managed Key Service
cards.teaser: Cloud Key Management Service is Google's managed keystore for symmetric and asymmetric cryptographic keys. It lets you create, rotate, import, and destroy keys without managing hardware, while keeping every key operation fully audited in Cloud Audit Logs.

runs.text: Cloud KMS

is a hosted key management service that stores cryptographic keys inside Google's infrastructure and exposes them through an API. Your application never sees the raw key bytes — you call KMS to encrypt or decrypt data, and the service returns the result. The key itself never leaves KMS.
The resource hierarchy inside KMS is:

items.text: Key ring
— a regional grouping of keys. Key rings are permanent; they cannot be deleted. Keys inherit the location of their ring.
CryptoKey
— the logical key object. It has a purpose (ENCRYPT_DECRYPT, ASYMMETRIC_SIGN, ASYMMETRIC_DECRYPT, MAC) and a rotation schedule.
CryptoKeyVersion
— the actual key material for a given rotation epoch. A CryptoKey can have many versions; one is the primary. Old versions can be kept for decryption but disabled for new encryption.

runs.text: Common gcloud commands:

items.text: gcloud kms keyrings create my-ring --location=us-central1
gcloud kms keys create my-key --keyring=my-ring --location=us-central1 --purpose=encryption
gcloud kms encrypt --key=my-key --keyring=my-ring --location=us-central1 --plaintext-file=secret.txt --ciphertext-file=secret.enc
gcloud kms decrypt --key=my-key --keyring=my-ring --location=us-central1 --ciphertext-file=secret.enc --plaintext-file=secret.txt

runs.text: Every encrypt and decrypt call is logged to Cloud Audit Logs (Data Access logs). Rotation is configured via
--rotation-period
and
--next-rotation-time
. Automatic rotation creates a new primary version; the old version continues to decrypt existing ciphertexts until explicitly destroyed.

Cloud KMS supports three protection levels: SOFTWARE (keys protected by Google's software layer), HSM (keys protected by FIPS 140-2 Level 3 hardware — see Cloud HSM card), and EXTERNAL / EXTERNAL_VPC for keys managed outside Google's infrastructure.

Cloud KMS is a lockbox service: you send your plaintext to it, it locks it with a key you own but never touch directly, and it hands back the locked version. To read the data later, you send the locked version back and KMS unlocks it for you.

cards.title: CMEK — Customer-Managed Encryption Keys
cards.teaser: CMEK lets you use your own Cloud KMS keys to encrypt data at rest in Google-managed services (Cloud Storage, BigQuery, Pub/Sub, GKE etcd, and many others). Google still manages the storage layer; you control the key — which means you can revoke access to your data at any time.

runs.text: By default, Google encrypts all data at rest using
Google-managed encryption keys (GMEK)

— keys that Google creates, rotates, and controls entirely. CMEK replaces the GMEK layer: you create a key in Cloud KMS and tell the Google service to use it when wrapping the service's own internal data encryption keys (envelope encryption).
How envelope encryption works with CMEK:

items.text: The Google service generates a per-object data encryption key (DEK) for each piece of data.
The DEK is wrapped (encrypted) using your CMEK key in Cloud KMS.
Only the wrapped DEK is stored alongside the data. The raw DEK is discarded.
To read data, the service calls KMS to unwrap the DEK, decrypts the data in memory, and returns it.

runs.text: The critical control CMEK provides:
revocation

. If you disable or destroy your KMS key version, the Google service can no longer unwrap DEKs, making all data encrypted with that key version inaccessible — to Google and to you. This is the mechanism behind regulatory requirements for cryptographic erasure.
Enabling CMEK for a Cloud Storage bucket:

items.text: Grant the GCS service account the
roles/cloudkms.cryptoKeyEncrypterDecrypter
role on the key.
gcloud storage buckets update gs://my-bucket --default-kms-key=projects/PROJECT/locations/REGION/keyRings/RING/cryptoKeys/KEY

runs.text: CMEK does not protect against a Google employee with storage-layer access — it is not designed for that threat model. Its primary value is compliance attestation (you control the key) and cryptographic erasure (revoke key = inaccessible data). For hardware-level key isolation, use Cloud HSM.

CMEK means Google still stores your data, but they must ask your key in Cloud KMS for permission to read it. If you revoke that permission by disabling the key, the data becomes unreadable — even to Google.

cards.title: CSEK — Customer-Supplied Encryption Keys
cards.teaser: CSEK is the bring-your-own-bytes model: you supply the raw 256-bit AES key material on every API request, and Google uses it only for that operation, storing nothing. It offers maximum key isolation but at high operational complexity — rarely used today.

runs.text: With CSEK, you generate the encryption key yourself (256-bit AES), base64-encode it, and pass it in the
x-goog-encryption-key
HTTP header on every Cloud Storage or Compute Engine disk operation. Google uses the key transiently — it is never written to persistent storage at Google's side.
The operational burden is significant:

items.text: You must present the key on every read and write. If you lose the key, data is permanently unrecoverable.
Key rotation requires re-encrypting all objects with the new key using the
rewriteObject
API — there is no server-side automated rotation.
No Cloud KMS audit trail for individual key operations — you own the key, you own the audit responsibility.
Limited service integration: CSEK works with Cloud Storage and Compute Engine persistent disks; it is not supported across the broader GCP service catalog.

runs.text: CSEK vs CMEK trade-off:

items.text: CSEK
— key bytes never enter Google's key management system. Maximum isolation, maximum operational burden.
CMEK
— key is stored in Cloud KMS (or Cloud HSM). Google can see the key reference but not read encrypted data without your key. Manageable rotation, audit trail, broad service support.

runs.text: In practice, CMEK with Cloud HSM provides stronger compliance guarantees than CSEK for most regulated workloads, because HSM gives hardware-level key protection plus KMS audit logs. CSEK's use cases have narrowed to environments where organizational policy prohibits keys from ever touching a cloud provider's systems — including its HSM fleet.

CSEK is like handing the hotel a key to your room for one night and taking it back when you leave — they use it once, then it's gone. You control the key bytes completely, but you have to carry them everywhere and you can never lose them.

cards.title: Secret Manager — Versioned Secret Storage
cards.teaser: Secret Manager is Google Cloud's purpose-built service for storing, accessing, and rotating secrets such as API keys, passwords, and TLS certificates. Secrets are versioned, IAM-gated, and encrypted at rest with CMEK support. It replaces environment variables and configuration files as the secure way to inject credentials into applications.

runs.text: A
secret
in Secret Manager is a named resource that holds one or more
versions
. Each version stores an immutable binary payload (up to 64 KiB). A secret might be named
database-password
and have versions 1 through 5, where version 5 is the latest rotation.
Core operations:

items.text: Create a secret:
gcloud secrets create db-password --replication-policy=automatic
Add a version:
echo -n 'my-secret-value' | gcloud secrets versions add db-password --data-file=-
Access the latest version:
gcloud secrets versions access latest --secret=db-password
Disable a version (without deleting):
gcloud secrets versions disable 3 --secret=db-password

runs.text: Access control is IAM-based. The key role is
roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor

— grant it to a service account and that identity can read secret versions, but cannot list or modify secrets. This lets you scope access precisely: a Cloud Run service gets accessor on its own secret, nothing else.
Secret Manager also supports:

items.text: Rotation notifications via Pub/Sub — publish a message when a secret is due for rotation.
Customer-managed encryption (CMEK) — wrap secret payloads with your own KMS key.
Regional secrets — replicate to specific regions to meet data residency requirements.
Audit logging — every access attempt is logged to Cloud Audit Logs (Data Access category).

runs.text: The recommended pattern for Kubernetes workloads is to mount secrets via the Secret Manager add-on for the GKE Config Connector or the Workload Identity-enabled External Secrets Operator, rather than copying secret values into Kubernetes Secret objects — which are only base64-encoded, not encrypted at rest by default.

Secret Manager is a versioned, access-controlled vault for credentials. Your app asks it for the latest version of a secret using its service account identity; it either has permission and gets the value, or it does not and gets a 403.

cards.title: Binary Authorization — Admission-Time Image Policy
cards.teaser: Binary Authorization is a policy enforcement service that prevents untrusted container images from being deployed to GKE, Cloud Run, or GKE Autopilot. It requires that images be signed by trusted attestors before admission — implementing software supply chain security at deploy time.

runs.text: Binary Authorization works at the Kubernetes admission controller layer. Before a pod is allowed to schedule, the admission webhook checks the cluster's
policy
to determine whether the image digest is approved. If the image lacks the required attestations, the pod is rejected.
The key concepts:

items.text: Attestor
— a named authority (e.g., "security-scanner", "qa-approval") that signs image digests. Attestors use Cloud KMS asymmetric keys (or PGP) to create signatures.
Attestation
— a signed statement that an attestor vouches for a specific image digest. Stored in Container Analysis (part of Artifact Registry).
Policy

— a project-level or cluster-level rule specifying which attestors must have signed an image before it can be deployed. Policies support allowlist patterns (e.g., allow all images from a specific Artifact Registry project) and require-attestation rules.

runs.text: A typical CI/CD integration:

items.text: CI pipeline builds and pushes the image to Artifact Registry, recording the digest.
A vulnerability scanner runs; if it passes, the CI pipeline creates an attestation using the attestor's KMS key.
The GKE policy requires that attestation. Any image without it is blocked at admission.

runs.text: Enable Binary Authorization on a GKE cluster:

items.text: gcloud container clusters update my-cluster --enable-binauthz --location=us-central1

runs.text: Binary Authorization enforces policy on image digests (sha256 hashes), not on tags. Never build policy around mutable tags like :latest — a tag can be repointed to a different, unsigned digest, bypassing attestation checks.

Binary Authorization is a bouncer at the GKE door: every container image needs a signed approval from trusted reviewers before it is allowed in. No signature, no deployment — regardless of who is doing the deploying.

cards.title: Confidential Computing — TEE-Based VMs
cards.teaser: Confidential VMs use hardware Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) to encrypt data in use — not just at rest and in transit. The CPU encrypts VM memory with a key that even the hypervisor and Google's infrastructure cannot access, implementing hardware-enforced isolation.

runs.text: Traditional cloud security encrypts data at rest (storage) and in transit (TLS).
Confidential Computing
adds a third dimension:
data in use
. While your VM is running, its memory is encrypted by the CPU itself, using keys managed inside the processor's secure hardware and never exposed to the hypervisor layer or to Google's operations.
Google Cloud Confidential VMs are built on two hardware TEE technologies:

items.text: AMD SEV-SNP (Secure Encrypted Virtualization — Secure Nested Paging)

— encrypts VM memory with per-VM keys generated inside the AMD Secure Processor. SNP adds memory integrity protection: any unauthorized modification to encrypted memory pages is detected and the VM halts.
Intel TDX (Trust Domain Extensions)
— Intel's equivalent, introduced with 4th-gen Xeon Scalable (Sapphire Rapids). TDX creates a hardware-isolated Trust Domain; the hypervisor cannot read or modify TD memory.

runs.text: Both technologies support
remote attestation

: a workload can cryptographically prove to a relying party (e.g., a Secret Manager equivalent) that it is running inside a genuine TEE with unmodified firmware, before secrets are released to it. This is the foundation of confidential multi-party computation.
Create a Confidential VM (AMD SEV-SNP):

items.text: gcloud compute instances create my-cvm --machine-type=n2d-standard-4 --confidential-compute --on-host-maintenance=TERMINATE --image-family=ubuntu-2204-lts --image-project=ubuntu-os-cloud

runs.text: Confidential VMs require machine types that support the underlying CPU technology: N2D (AMD) for SEV/SEV-SNP, C3 (Intel) for TDX. Standard live migration is not available; you must set --on-host-maintenance=TERMINATE. There is typically a 0–6% performance overhead for memory-bound workloads.

A Confidential VM runs inside a locked vault inside the CPU itself. Even the cloud provider's hypervisor cannot read the VM's memory — the CPU hardware encrypts it and only gives the decryption key to the VM's own workload.

cards.title: Confidential GKE Nodes — TEE for Kubernetes Workloads
cards.teaser: Confidential GKE Nodes bring Confidential VM technology to Kubernetes worker nodes: every node in the node pool runs as a Confidential VM, encrypting pod memory at the hardware level. Kubernetes control-plane operations see only encrypted memory, providing TEE-level isolation for containerized workloads.

runs.text: Confidential GKE Nodes extend Confidential VM protections to GKE node pools. When you enable confidential nodes on a node pool, Google provisions each node as an AMD SEV-SNP or Intel TDX Confidential VM. All pods scheduled to those nodes run inside an encrypted memory domain.
The threat model addressed: a GKE node pool operator or a process with hypervisor-level access cannot read pod memory. Confidential GKE Nodes are relevant when:

items.text: Processing regulated data (PII, health records, financial data) and regulatory frameworks require hardware-level isolation.
Multi-tenant clusters where different tenants have strong isolation requirements.
Confidential machine learning: training or inferring on sensitive datasets where model and data must remain encrypted even during computation.

runs.text: Create a Confidential node pool:

items.text: gcloud container node-pools create confidential-pool --cluster=my-cluster --machine-type=n2d-standard-4 --enable-confidential-nodes --location=us-central1

runs.text: Confidential GKE Nodes integrate with Binary Authorization and Workload Identity: pods running on confidential nodes can produce TEE attestations to prove to downstream systems that their workload is running in a genuine hardware-protected environment.

Confidential GKE Nodes are compatible with GKE Autopilot as well as Standard mode. In Autopilot, enable the feature at cluster creation: gcloud container clusters create-auto my-cluster --enable-confidential-nodes. Node-level access to unencrypted memory is prevented by the hardware; Kubernetes etcd encryption and Pod Security Standards address the control plane and pod API layers separately.

Confidential GKE Nodes are Kubernetes worker nodes where the CPU hardware encrypts the memory of every running pod. Even someone with physical or hypervisor access to the machine cannot read what the containers are processing.

cards.title: Cloud HSM — FIPS 140-2 Level 3 Hardware Security Module
cards.teaser: Cloud HSM is a managed hardware security module service integrated with Cloud KMS. Keys stored in Cloud HSM are protected by FIPS 140-2 Level 3-validated hardware — they never exist in software, cannot be exported, and are physically protected against tampering inside the HSM hardware.

runs.text: Cloud HSM is not a separate product you interact with directly — it is a
protection level
within Cloud KMS. When you create a Cloud KMS key with
--protection-level=hsm

, the key material is generated inside and stored inside FIPS 140-2 Level 3 certified HSM hardware. All cryptographic operations happen inside the HSM; the raw key bytes never leave the hardware boundary.
FIPS 140-2 Level 3 requirements include:

items.text: Physical tamper-evidence and tamper-resistance: the HSM detects and responds to physical intrusion attempts by zeroizing key material.
Identity-based authentication for all cryptographic roles.
Role-based access control separating administration from cryptographic operations.

runs.text: Create an HSM-protected key:

items.text: gcloud kms keys create my-hsm-key --keyring=my-ring --location=us-central1 --purpose=encryption --protection-level=hsm

runs.text: From the API and IAM perspective, an HSM-backed key behaves identically to a software-backed KMS key. The difference is entirely in the hardware trust boundary. HSM keys support the same operations — encrypt, decrypt, sign, verify — with the same IAM controls and audit logging. Latency is slightly higher (typically 1–5 ms additional) due to hardware offload.
Cloud HSM is the right choice when:

items.text: Compliance mandates require FIPS 140-2 Level 3 (PCI DSS, FedRAMP High, certain HIPAA interpretations).
Your threat model includes insider access to Google's software key management infrastructure.
You need a non-exportable root of trust for certificate authorities or code signing.

runs.text: Cloud HSM is a shared HSM fleet, not a dedicated appliance. If your compliance framework requires a dedicated HSM with sole tenancy, use Cloud External Key Manager (Cloud EKM) with your own on-premises or dedicated HSM appliance instead.

Cloud HSM means your encryption keys live inside a tamper-proof hardware box that physically destroys itself if someone tries to pry it open. The key never leaves the hardware, and the hardware is certified by FIPS to prove it.

cards.title: Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP) — Zero-Trust Access to Apps
cards.teaser: IAP enforces identity- and context-based access control at the application layer, replacing perimeter-based VPN access for internal web apps and SSH/TCP tunneling. A user's identity and device posture are verified on every request before traffic reaches the backend.

runs.text: Traditional access control for internal applications relies on network perimeter (VPN): if you are inside the VPN, you can reach internal resources. IAP inverts this model. The VPN perimeter is replaced by identity verification at the HTTP(S) load balancer layer —
every request
is authenticated, regardless of network location.
How IAP works for HTTPS apps:

items.text: A user navigates to the app's URL. IAP sits in front of the Google Load Balancer.
IAP redirects unauthenticated users to Google Sign-In (OAuth 2.0).
After authentication, IAP checks whether the authenticated identity has the IAM role
roles/iap.httpsResourceAccessor
on the IAP resource.
If authorized, the request is forwarded to the backend with a signed JWT (
X-Goog-IAP-JWT-Assertion
header) containing the user's identity. The backend can validate this JWT without any additional auth logic.

runs.text: IAP also supports TCP tunneling for SSH and other non-HTTP protocols:

items.text: gcloud compute ssh my-instance --tunnel-through-iap
— SSHes to a VM through IAP without requiring a public IP or VPN connection.
gcloud compute start-iap-tunnel my-instance 3306 --local-host-port=localhost:3306
— creates an IAP TCP tunnel to a Cloud SQL proxy port.

runs.text: IAP integrates with BeyondCorp Enterprise for device trust: access can be conditioned not just on identity but on device policy (OS patch level, certificate presence, endpoint verification agent).

IAP only protects traffic that goes through the Google-managed load balancer. A VM with a public IP and a firewall rule allowing direct port 80/443 access bypasses IAP entirely. Enforce IAP protection by allowing only the load balancer's IP ranges (and the IAP forwarder range 35.235.240.0/20) in VPC firewall rules.

IAP is a Google-managed bouncer in front of your app. Instead of giving everyone on the corporate VPN a free pass, it checks each person's Google identity and IAM role on every request. No identity match, no access — regardless of which network they are on.

cards.title: BeyondCorp Enterprise — Google's Zero Trust Architecture
cards.teaser: BeyondCorp Enterprise is Google Cloud's Zero Trust access product, combining IAP, device trust enforcement, threat intelligence, and DLP-enabled Chrome browser controls. It is the commercial implementation of the BeyondCorp model Google developed internally and described in a series of papers beginning in 2014.

runs.text: Google's BeyondCorp project began in 2011 in response to Operation Aurora, a sophisticated attack that compromised several major technology companies via network perimeter failures. The principle, described across six papers published in USENIX ;login: and ACM Queue (2014–2020), is:
access to services should be granted based on what you know about the user and the device, not where the request originates on the network.
The seminal paper, "BeyondCorp: A New Approach to Enterprise Security" (Ward and Beyer, Google, 2014), defined three control planes:

items.text: Device inventory service
— tracks every managed and unmanaged device, its OS, patch level, and certificate.
User and group database
— the authoritative source for identity.
Access proxy
— enforces policy at the application layer, combining user identity + device trust signals for every request.

runs.text: BeyondCorp Enterprise (BCE) is the GCP product that commercializes this model. Its components:

items.text: Identity-Aware Proxy
— the access proxy layer (see prior card).
Endpoint Verification
— a Chrome extension and OS agent that reports device posture (encryption, screen lock, OS version, policy compliance) to Google's device inventory.
Access Context Manager
— defines access levels and perimeters. An access level is a boolean condition combining user identity, device attributes, IP range, and time.
Chrome Enterprise Premium (formerly Chrome Enterprise)
— managed browser with DLP controls, threat intelligence, and data loss prevention for SaaS apps.

runs.text: A BCE access policy might read: "Allow access to the finance app only for users in the finance group, on a managed device running macOS 14+ with full-disk encryption enabled, from an IP not on the threat intelligence block list." Every one of those conditions is evaluated per-request.

The full BeyondCorp paper series is publicly available: beyondcorp.com. The six papers cover the original model, how Google migrated 60,000 employees off VPN over five years, the enterprise components, cloud-based access, and the move to a more general BeyondProd model for service-to-service authentication.

BeyondCorp Enterprise replaces the VPN with a policy engine: to access any application you need the right identity plus a device that passes a health check. Being inside the office network gives you nothing; being on an unknown or non-compliant device blocks you even if your identity is valid.

cards.title: Cloud Identity — IdP and Directory Service
cards.teaser: Cloud Identity is Google's standalone identity provider and directory service for organizations that use Google Cloud but not Google Workspace. It provides managed Google accounts for users and groups, enables SSO and MFA, and is the identity foundation for IAM, BeyondCorp, and MDM — without the Workspace productivity apps.

runs.text: Many GCP IAM and security features require that users and groups be represented as
Google Identities
(managed by Google's identity system). Cloud Identity provides this for organizations that use GCP but have not purchased Google Workspace (formerly G Suite).
Cloud Identity vs Google Workspace:

items.text: Google Workspace
— identity + Gmail, Google Drive, Google Meet, Google Docs, and all productivity apps. Per-user licensing cost.
Cloud Identity Free
— managed Google accounts, groups, SSO, basic MDM. Up to 50 free accounts per domain. No Workspace apps.
Cloud Identity Premium
— adds advanced MDM, app access control, endpoint verification, and audit logging. The tier required for BeyondCorp Enterprise device management.

runs.text: Key capabilities Cloud Identity provides:

items.text: SAML 2.0 and OIDC federation
— federate an existing corporate IdP (Okta, Azure AD, Ping) into Google identities. Users log in through their corporate SSO; Google receives a trusted assertion.
Google Groups
— the primary IAM principal for team-based access. Assign IAM roles to groups, not individuals, to simplify access management.
Context-Aware Access
— integrates device trust signals into IAP and Workspace application access.
Directory sync (GCDS)
— Google Cloud Directory Sync replicates users and groups from an on-premises LDAP/Active Directory into Cloud Identity on a schedule.

runs.text: Cloud Identity is the recommended approach for organizations that bring an existing enterprise directory (Active Directory, LDAP) to GCP. The pattern is: sync users with GCDS, federate authentication with SAML so users keep their existing corporate login, and use the resulting Google identities to bind IAM roles.

Cloud Identity gives your employees Google accounts without buying Google Workspace. Those accounts are then the identities that Google Cloud's IAM, IAP, and BeyondCorp recognize — connecting your corporate directory to GCP's access control layer.

cards.title: reCAPTCHA Enterprise — Bot Detection and Risk Scoring
cards.teaser: reCAPTCHA Enterprise is Google's bot-detection and fraud-prevention service for web and mobile applications. Unlike consumer reCAPTCHA v3, it is designed for enterprise integrations: it returns a risk score and rich signals rather than a pass/fail result, enabling fine-grained action policies without user friction.

runs.text: reCAPTCHA Enterprise assesses every interaction — form submission, login attempt, checkout, account creation — and returns a
risk score
between 0.0 (very likely bot) and 1.0 (very likely human), along with structured
reasons
such as
AUTOMATION
UNEXPECTED_ENVIRONMENT
, or
TOO_MUCH_TRAFFIC
Integration flow:

items.text: Embed the reCAPTCHA Enterprise JavaScript snippet in your page. When a user interacts, the client runs a local risk assessment and generates a
token
Your server submits the token to the reCAPTCHA Enterprise API via
projects.assessments.create
The API returns an Assessment with a risk score, reasons, and (for checkbox reCAPTCHA) a validity signal.
Your application enforces policy based on the score: allow, challenge, block, require MFA, flag for review.

runs.text: Enterprise-specific capabilities beyond consumer reCAPTCHA v3:

items.text: Account Defender
— tracks account-level behavior across sessions to detect credential stuffing and account takeover patterns.
Password Leak Detection
— checks submitted credentials against known-breached password databases without exposing the credentials to Google.
Firewall integration
— Cloud Armor can consume reCAPTCHA Enterprise tokens and enforce score-based WAF rules at the load balancer layer, before requests reach the application.
Mobile SDK
— Android and iOS SDKs provide the same scoring for native mobile apps, addressing bot activity on mobile APIs.

runs.text: reCAPTCHA Enterprise is billed per assessment. There is no challenge displayed to users for score-based assessments (the friction model); the score is invisible. Only explicit checkbox or audio challenge modes show UI. This allows high-volume assessment of every login or form submission without affecting user experience for legitimate users.

reCAPTCHA Enterprise watches how a user interacts with your page and scores the session from 0 to 1. Your backend then decides what to do with that score: let the request through, ask for an extra auth step, or block it — no checkbox required for the user to see.

cards.title: Security Command Center — Central Posture Management
cards.teaser: Security Command Center (SCC) is Google Cloud's centralized security and risk management platform. It aggregates vulnerability findings, misconfiguration alerts, threat detections, and compliance posture across all GCP resources in an organization, providing a single pane of glass for security operations.

runs.text: SCC operates at the
organization

level — it can see across all projects and folders, unlike project-scoped tools. This is critical: multi-project GCP organizations need cross-project visibility to detect lateral movement, over-permissioned service accounts, and publicly exposed storage buckets at scale.
SCC has two tiers:

items.text: Standard (free)
— Security Health Analytics (misconfiguration detection), Web Security Scanner for App Engine and Cloud Run URLs, and integration with partner security tools.
Premium / Enterprise

— adds Event Threat Detection (ETD), Container Threat Detection, Virtual Machine Threat Detection, Attack path simulation, Compliance posture dashboards (CIS, PCI DSS, NIST), and Findings export to Chronicle SIEM.

runs.text: Key integrated services that feed findings into SCC:

items.text: Security Health Analytics
— continuously scans resource configurations for CIS Benchmark violations: public Cloud Storage buckets, overly broad IAM bindings, unencrypted disks, open firewall rules.
Event Threat Detection (ETD)
— analyzes Cloud Audit Logs and Cloud DNS logs for indicators of compromise: unusual service account activity, crypto mining, data exfiltration patterns, brute force attempts.
Container Threat Detection
— monitors GKE node kernel for suspicious container behaviors: unexpected child processes, reverse shell execution, cryptomining binaries.
Virtual Machine Threat Detection
— scans VM memory from the hypervisor layer without requiring an agent, detecting rootkits and cryptomining malware.

runs.text: Findings can be exported to Pub/Sub for integration with SIEM systems (Splunk, Chronicle) or used to trigger automated remediation via Cloud Functions or Security Health Analytics Automated Remediation:

items.text: gcloud scc findings list ORGANIZATION_ID --filter='state=ACTIVE AND severity=CRITICAL'

runs.text: SCC Enterprise (released 2024) unifies SCC with Mandiant threat intelligence and Chronicle SIEM into a single product, providing Google Threat Intelligence integration, managed detection and response (MDR) capabilities, and AI-assisted triage. It represents the convergence of GCP-native security posture management with enterprise SIEM and threat hunting capabilities.

Security Command Center is the dashboard where you see every security problem across all your GCP projects in one place: the storage bucket someone left public, the VM with a rootkit, the service account with owner-level access it should not have. It finds the problems; your team fixes them.
